title: Pair in a Sorted List
statement:
You get an array of integers nums that is sorted in non-decreasing order, and an integer target. Find the two different positions i and j whose values add up to target.

Exactly one such pair of positions exists. A position cannot be used twice, but two positions may hold equal values.

Return [i, j] as 0-based indexes with i < j. Use only O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: 1 + 6 = 7. The ends give -4 + 10 = 6, too small, so the left end moves up and never comes back.
The two 5s sit at different positions, so they form a valid pair.
4 + 4 would be 8, but there is only one 4. The answer is 2 + 6.

constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
Exactly one pair of positions adds up to target
hints: A hash map solves the unsorted version in O(n) time but O(n) memory. What does the sorted order give you instead?
Look at the smallest and the largest value. If their sum is too small, can the smallest value be part of the answer with anything?
Keep a pointer at each end. Sum too small: move the left pointer right. Too big: move the right pointer left. Equal: done.

explain.intuition:
Take the smallest value nums[lo] and the largest nums[hi]. If their sum is too small, then nums[lo] plus anything else is also too small, because everything else is ≤ nums[hi]. So nums[lo] can never be in the answer, and you drop it. The same argument drops nums[hi] when the sum is too big. Each step removes one candidate, so after at most n steps you reach the pair.

The point of this version is memory. The complement-map solution is already O(n) time, but it stores up to n values. Here the sorted order does the job of the map, and you need two integers. That matters when the data is large or lives somewhere you can only scan, such as a sorted file or a virtualised list you read from both ends.
steps: If sum < target, the left value is too small for every remaining partner: lo++. Otherwise hi--.
Repeat. The guarantee of one answer means the loop always finds it before lo meets hi.
pitfalls: Using a hash map anyway. It passes on time but breaks the O(1) memory rule, which is the whole point of this problem.
Binary searching the complement from position i instead of i + 1: in [1, 6, 6] with target 12, the search for 6 can land on the first 6 itself and return [1, 1]. Search only to the right of i.
Returning 1-based indexes out of habit. This version asks for 0-based.

solutions.title: Try every pair
solutions.idea: Two nested loops over i < j. Ignores the sorted order completely.

solutions.title: Binary search for each complement
solutions.idea: For each i, binary search target − nums[i] in the part of the array to the right of i. Uses the order, still O(1) memory, but pays a log factor.

solutions.title: Two pointers from the ends
solutions.idea: Start at both ends. A small sum means the left value is useless, a big sum means the right value is useless. Drop one per step.

followups: Count how many pairs of positions add up to target, with duplicates allowed. How do you handle runs of equal values?
Find the pair whose sum is closest to target without going over it.
